Let me carefully analyze this candidate proof for IMO 2026 Problem 1.

The problem: 2026 integers > 1 on a blackboard. A move: choose two integers m, n > 1 from different places, replace with gcd(m,n) and lcm(m,n)/gcd(m,n). Continue while possible. Prove: (a) process terminates with exactly one integer M > 1; (b) M doesn't depend on choices.

Let me verify the key claims.

**Termination proof:**

Board state: entries x_1, ..., x_2026. P = product, K = number of entries > 1.

Move on m, n > 1: new entries are g = gcd(m,n) and lcm(m,n)/g = mn/g².

Product of new entries: g · (mn/g²) = mn/g. So new board product P' = P/g.

- If g > 1: P' < P. K may change: if g = m (i.e., m | n), then first new entry is m > 1, second is n/m which could be 1 (if n = m) or > 1. So K can decrease or stay same. But P decreases, so lexicographic pair decreases.
- If g = 1: new entries are 1 and mn. P' = P. Both m, n > 1 contributed 2 to K; new entries: 1 (not counted) and mn > 1 (counted once). So K' = K - 1. Good.

So (P, K) lex strictly decreases. P is a positive integer that never increases; each P-decrease can happen only finitely often; between P-decreases, K strictly decreases and K ≥ 1 (well, K ≥ 0), so finitely many moves. Actually more carefully: P takes finitely many values (divisors of initial P), each value of P allows at most K ≤ 2026 moves. So total moves ≤ 2026 · (number of distinct P values) — finite. Termination holds regardless of choices. ✓.

Terminal state: no legal move possible means at most one entry > 1. And a move never eliminates all nonunits: if g > 1, output g > 1; if g = 1, output mn > 1. Initially all 2026 entries > 1, so at least one nonunit persists. Hence exactly one M > 1 at the end. ✓.

**Invariant / value of M:**

Fix prime p. Move replaces exponents (a, b) with (min(a,b), |a−b|). Claim: gcd of the whole exponent vector is invariant.

gcd of all entries: replacing a, b by min(a,b) and |a−b|. We need gcd(rest, a, b) = gcd(rest, min(a,b), |a−b|). Since gcd(a,b) = gcd(min(a,b), |a−b|) (standard: gcd(a,b) = gcd(a, b−a) for a ≤ b; also gcd(a, b−a) where both could be zero: gcd(0,0) = 0 by convention). So gcd(rest, a, b) = gcd(rest, gcd(a,b)) = gcd(rest, gcd(min(a,b), |a−b|)) = gcd(rest, min(a,b), |a−b|). ✓. So G_p = gcd(e_1, ..., e_2026) invariant.

At terminal board, entries are M, 1, ..., 1. Exponent vector for p: (v_p(M), 0, ..., 0). gcd = v_p(M). Hence v_p(M) = G_p for every prime p. ✓. So M = ∏ p^{G_p}. Unique, independent of choices. ✓.

Also note: G_p is nonzero only for primes dividing at least one A_i — finitely many. ✓.

Wait — one subtle point: the final M > 1 exists and is unique; also the formula gives M ≥ 1. Is it possible that all G_p = 0, giving M = 1, contradicting the existence of a nonunit? Initially all entries > 1, so for each initial entry there's some prime; but G_p = gcd over all entries — could all G_p be 0? G_p = 0 iff all v_p(A_i) = 0. Since A_1 > 1, some prime p divides A_1, and then G_p ≥ v_p(A_1)... wait, gcd includes v_p(A_1) ≥ 1, so G_p = gcd(..., v_p(A_1), ...) which divides v_p(A_1)? No — gcd of a set including a positive number and zeros: gcd(0, ..., 0, e, 0, ..., 0) = e. If other entries have 0, gcd is still e? gcd(0, e) = e. Yes. Hmm wait, gcd(0, e) = e. So if p divides only A_1 and not others, the gcd of the exponent vector is still v_p(A_1) because gcd(0, x) = x. So G_p = gcd of all = gcd of nonzero ones (zeros don't affect gcd except when all zero). So G_p > 0 whenever some entry has p. Since A_1 > 1 has some prime, some G_p > 0, hence M > 1. Consistent. ✓ (This matches the persistence argument: terminal board has exactly one nonunit, so M > 1, and indeed formula gives M > 1.)

Edge cases: m = n (equal values in different places allowed). g = m, second = 1. Exponents (a,a) ↦ (a, 0). gcd preserved: gcd(a,a) = a = gcd(a, 0). ✓. Also K: two nonunits become one nonunit (m) and 1; K decreases by 1; P decreases by factor g = m > 1. Fine.

Coprime m, n: g = 1, second = mn. P unchanged, K decreases by 1. Fine.

The descent measure: lex (P, K). Need well-foundedness: P strictly decreases at most finitely many times since P is a positive integer; K decreases while P fixed, K a nonneg integer. So no infinite descent. ✓. Actually potential subtlety: when g > 1, does K possibly increase? New entries: g > 1 (counts), mn/g² which is ≥ 1; could mn/g² > 1 even when... both m,n > 1 counted 2 before; after: g counts 1, mn/g² counts 1 if > 1. So K' − K ∈ {0, −1}. Never increases.
